english: Coffee / make coffee
keywords: Coffee / make coffee coffea, coffeae f. english: Smoothie / juice / pulp / flavour / thick / thin

english: Blender / blender jug / lid / blade / button / appliance
keywords: Blender / blender jug / lid / blade / button / appliance māchina concīsōria Lexicographic evidence Modern application māchina, māchinae f.; māchina concīsōria — machine; blender. Traupman explicitly gives this appliance name. māchina mixtōria; māchina liquātōria — recorded alternative blender names in Morgan–Owens; not names for ancient appliances. urceus, urceī m.; urceus māchinae — jug; the blender jug, our descriptive application. operculum, operculī n.; lāmina, lāminae f. — lid; blade or thin plate. Lāmina here is applied to a blender blade. basis, basis f.; manūbrium, manūbriī n. — base; handle. globulus, globulī m. — small knob or button; applied here to the control button. Operculum claude. Globulum preme. — Close the lid. Press the button. operculum, operculī n. also covers a container’s cap, not only a blender lid; Morgan–Owens explicitly groups “lid, cap (of container).” For a cap worn on the head, see pilleus . Operculum impōne. — Put the lid / cap on. The headword māchina concīsōria was visually verified in Traupman, printed p. 280 (PDF p. 281). Labels for the jug, base and control are transparent modern applications of older nouns, not independently attested names for this particular blender. keywords: Grate / grind / crush / blend / mix / stir rādō, rādere · conterō, conterere · misceō, miscēre Ancient verbs Modern blender use rādō, rādere, rāsī, rāsum — scrape; applied to grating with a rādula. terō, terere, trīvī, trītum; conterō, conterere, contrīvī, contrītum — grind or rub down; grind or crush thoroughly. misceō, miscēre, miscuī, mixtum — mix or blend; mixing alone need not imply that solid pieces have been ground smooth. agitō, agitāre — stir or agitate in an appropriate cooking context. keywords: smoothie smoothies preparation Nutrition / protein / fibre / fat / calcium / sugar / vitamins nūtrītiō, nūtrītiōnis f. nūtrītiō, nūtrītiōnis f.; pars nūtriēns, partis nūtrientis f. — nutrition or nourishing; nutrient, with a descriptive part-that-nourishes phrase recorded by Morgan–Owens. proteīnum, proteīnī n. — protein; recorded in Morgan–Owens’s Silva through Helfer/Heyse. The checked entry marks ī but does not establish every stem quantity. fībra, fībrae f.; fībrae alimentāriae — fibre; dietary fibre, our modern technical description. Lewis & Short allows variation in the first vowel of fībra; we use the long-vowel reading here. Classical fibra by itself does not specifically mean dietary fibre. adeps, adipis m. or f. — fat; applied in a nutritional context. calcium, calciī n.; saccharum, saccharī n. — calcium; sugar. The chemical-element sense is modern; saccharum is ancient. vītamīnum, vītamīnī n.; vītamīna D et B12 — vitamin; vitamins D and B12. The existing vitamin entry explains the adopted reading convention. vīs, vīs f.; vīrēs, vīrium f. pl. — strength or power; energy in a broad everyday sense, not a precise unit of food energy. These names let us discuss the guide without turning modern nutritional categories into supposedly Classical concepts. Chemical and loanword quantities remain limited to the checked evidence.

english: Make smoothies with Theo / choose / wash / prepare / cut together
keywords: smoothie smoothies preparation Make smoothies with Theo / choose / wash / prepare / cut together Potiōnem ūnā parēmus. Theodōre, potiōnem ūnā parēmus. — Theo, let’s make a smoothie together. Quae pōma ēligimus? Pirum an mālum? — Which fruit shall we choose? A pear or an apple? Vīs potiōnem viridem an dulcem? — Would you like a green smoothie or a sweet one? Prīmum manūs lavēmus. — First, let’s wash our hands. Tū pōma lavā; ego secābō. — You wash the fruit; I’ll do the cutting. Cucumerem mihi porrige, quaesō. — Pass me the cucumber, please. Hoc est incīsōrium; haec est rādula. — This is the cutting board; this is the grater. Cavē tibi. Culter acūtus est. — Be careful. The knife is sharp. Pōma in frūstula secēmus. — Let’s cut the fruit into small pieces. Frūstula in urceum pōne. — Put the pieces into the jug. All sentences are composed for the family. The prompts draw on the ingredient, tool and preparation entries above; they are not quotations from Traupman or Morgan–Owens.

keywords: smoothie smoothies preparation Blend with Theo / taste / share / drink / clean up Nunc omnia conterāmus. english: White cheese / yellow cheese / banitsa / tarator / lyutenitsa
keywords: White cheese / yellow cheese / banitsa / tarator / lyutenitsa cāseus albus · placenta, placentae f. Ancient words Modern descriptions cāseus albus (muriā condītus) — sirene, the Bulgarian white brined cheese (Bulg. сирене); our description, brined on the model of Catō’s green olives (Agr. 7, 4: conduntur … viridēs in muriā). cāseus flāvus — kashkaval, the firm yellow cheese (Bulg. кашкавал); our description. placenta, placentae f. — Catō’s layered cake of dough sheets (tracta) and cheese, built sheet by sheet (Agr. 76, ūsus: Culīna; Hor. Ep. I 10, 11) — the nearest ancient thing to banitsa (Bulg. баница). placenta cāseō farta — a cheese-filled banitsa. iūs frīgidum ex iogurtō cucumereque — tarator, the cold yogurt-and-cucumber soup (Bulg. таратор); our description. For the yogurt loan see the iogurtum entry. condīmentum ex piperītidibus trītīs — lyutenitsa, the roasted-pepper relish (Bulg. лютеница); our description. Māne placentam calidam ēmimus. — In the morning we buy a warm banitsa. placenta is attested and genuinely layered, so it carries the banitsa idea honestly; the Romanian plăcintă family continues the Latin word, while баница itself is Slavic. The Bulgarian dishes are given descriptions, not forced coinages.
